findings.claim: Removing the `valueOf`/`toString`/`toJSON` short-circuit reintroduces the coercion bug it was added to fix: any implicit string/primitive conversion of the proxy (React 19 rendering, template literals, `console.log`, `JSON.stringify`) will now fall through to `callback({ args, path })` with a path ending in `toString`/`valueOf`/`toJSON`, issuing a bogus tRPC request (or returning a non-primitive, which makes `String(proxy)` throw `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value`).
findings.rationale: The `get` trap of this proxy returns a nested proxy for every key, so `proxy.toString` is callable and `apply` is the only place that could intercept the coercion call. With this block gone there is no interception left, so the previously fixed behavior regresses. I'm fairly confident about the mechanism; the only uncertainty is whether a replacement guard was added elsewhere in the file (e.g. a `Symbol.toPrimitive`/`toString` case in the `get` trap) outside this hunk — worth verifying before merging.

findings.claim: With the guard removed, `path` can now be empty in `apply` (e.g. `proxyInstance()` called directly), making `lastOfPath` `undefined` and passing an empty `path` array into `callback`; the previous block at least short-circuited a common class of such calls.
findings.rationale: Secondary/lower-confidence observation: the removed block did not itself null-guard `path`, but it did intercept the most common accidental invocations. Downstream consumers that assume `path.length > 0` may now receive malformed opts. Worth a quick check of the callback implementations.
